access: Unauthorized access to the Mt. Gox server in Japan that held the exchange's wallets and private keys (DOJ indictments, unsealed June 2023)
detection: Not detected for about 2.5 years; the theft ran from about September 2011 to at least May 2014 and surfaced when Mt. Gox halted and filed for bankruptcy in February 2014
response: Exchange collapsed (2014 bankruptcy); two Russian nationals charged (2019 indictments, unsealed 2023)
ibs_note: Raw keys taken from the server (S1), so the signer's checks are bypassed. The drain was slow and lasted years, the A8 pattern, which per-window budgets (C3) do not trip; only a watcher reconciling on-chain outflows against the ledger (C4) catches it. On Bitcoin both controls need a policy co-signer or script, not a single key.
disputed: USD value depends on the date. The DOJ gives 647,000 BTC stolen 2011-2014; $470M is the DeFiLlama figure (valuation at the 2014 collapse), not re-derived here

access: The attacker obtained the private key of the hot wallet holding all of Coincheck's NEM (Coincheck press conference); how it was obtained was not disclosed in the sources used
detection: About 8.5 hours after the first transfer (about 18:00 UTC Jan 25); Coincheck noticed an abnormal balance drop
response: Trading and most withdrawals halted; the NEM Foundation tagged tainted accounts; Coincheck reimbursed about 260,000 users from its own funds; reported to police and Japan's FSA
ibs_note: All NEM sat in one single-key hot wallet, not a multisig. With raw key theft (S1) the signer's checks are bypassed; a policy co-signer enforcing a per-window budget (C3) would have capped the drain, and a watcher (C4) would have closed the 8.5-hour detection gap.

access: Disputed. The owner blamed a flaw in Nano's software; the Nano team, and the Italian bankruptcy court's technical expert as reported, point to BitGrail's own withdrawal software, which allowed double withdrawals
detection: BitGrail announced on Feb 9, 2018 that internal checks had found a 17M XRB shortfall; withdrawals had been restricted in the preceding weeks
response: Exchange closed; an Italian court declared it bankrupt and seized the owner's assets (ruling made public January 2019)
ibs_controls: C1, C3 (only if the exchange's own software signed withdrawals that exceeded user balances)
ibs_note: If the Nano team and the court are right, the custodian's own system signed withdrawals that no ledger balance supported; binding each withdrawal to an intent checked against the ledger by an independent authority (C1) and a per-window budget (C3) target exactly that. If a protocol flaw was the cause, IBS does not apply.
disputed: Cause (exchange software vs Nano protocol). Start date: the date field is the disclosure date; victims' filings say the losses began in October 2017

chains: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Dogecoin, XRP, Zcash, Litecoin, Ethereum Classic
access: Alleged use of the exchange's private keys by DPRK-linked actors (ZachXBT on-chain analysis, November 2022)
detection: Never disclosed by Gate.io; made public by ZachXBT in November 2022
response: Gate.io did not confirm and deflected questions (CryptoSlate)
ibs_note: Only one independent analysis exists (ZachXBT, relayed by the press); Lookonchain adds only that Gate.io's hot wallet's first transaction is dated April 21, 2018. The victim has not confirmed, and the authorization path is unknown. Listed, not evaluated.
disputed: Date given as April 21 (ZachXBT, Lookonchain) and April 18 (CryptoSlate)

access: Phishing, viruses and other attacks against users to obtain many user API keys, 2FA codes and other data
detection: The withdrawal triggered internal alarms after it executed; withdrawals stopped immediately afterwards
response: Deposits and withdrawals suspended for about a week; loss covered by the SAFU fund
ibs_note: Withdrawals were requested through genuine but stolen user credentials, so the exchange's own system signed them. IBS binds signatures to user-authenticated intents, which does not help when the user's own authentication is stolen; an exposure budget (C3) on a single 7,000 BTC transaction and pre-execution anomaly checks are the relevant controls. Partial coverage.

chains: Bitcoin, Ethereum and ERC-20 tokens, Tron, XRP, Stellar and others
access: Advanced persistent threat inside KuCoin's internal network; the attacker obtained the private keys of several hot wallets (CEO letter, February 2021)
detection: KuCoin's risk system alerted at 03:01 UTC+8 on Sept 26 (Sept 25 UTC); shutting down the wallet server at 03:20 did not stop the transfers
response: Deposits and withdrawals suspended. About $204M was out of the attacker's control within two weeks, and $239M (84%) was eventually recovered with issuers, exchanges and law enforcement; the insurance fund covered the rest
ibs_note: Transfers continued after KuCoin shut its wallet server: the keys were used outside its signing system, so the signer's checks (C1, C2) could not act (S1). On-chain budgets (C3) and a freeze (C4) would; here containment came from token issuers and exchanges freezing funds after the fact.
disputed: The DeFiLlama dataset dates the incident Sept 29; KuCoin's timeline starts Sept 26 UTC+8

access: Weak private-key generation; keys brute-forced by an unknown actor (Arkham; MilkSad research). Alternative account in the disputed field
detection: Never reported by LuBian; made public by Arkham in August 2025. LuBian sent OP_RETURN messages to the receiving addresses asking for the funds back
response: LuBian moved about 11,886 BTC to recovery wallets by Dec 31, 2020. In October 2025 the DOJ filed to forfeit about 127,271 BTC as proceeds of the Prince Group's fraud and described them as the bitcoins "stolen" from LuBian
ibs_note: If this was weak-key theft, key generation is outside IBS (correctly generated keys are assumed), and with raw keys (S1) only script-level limits and monitoring help. If it was an internal movement between Prince Group wallets, it is out of scope (S3). Excluded from evaluated totals.
attacker_model: A6 if weak-key theft; none if internal
disputed: Whether a theft occurred. Arkham and MilkSad describe an unknown actor exploiting weak keys. The DOJ treats the coins as Chen Zhi's and does not say how the US obtained the keys, which leaves open compromise, surrender or an internal move. China's CVERC alleges US state hacking; CryptoSlate finds no credible evidence for that

access: A crafted cross-chain message made EthCrossChainManager call EthCrossChainData.putCurEpochConPubKeyBytes (a function-selector collision), which replaced the keeper public key with the attacker's
detection: Same day
response: The attacker returned about $342M within hours and nearly all funds over the following days
ibs_note: Contract access-control bug (S2). Notable for IBS: the bug let the attacker install its own key as the bridge's keeper, so every later unlock was validly signed. A per-window budget (C3) on the lock proxy would still have capped the drain.

access: Leaked administrator private key for BXH's BNB Chain deployment (BXH, PeckShield). The CEO suggested an insider; a later BXH-commissioned investigation (Bit Jungle, press release) pointed to an external party
detection: Same day; BXH announced it on Oct 30
response: Withdrawals halted; contracts on other chains locked; case filed with Chinese police; bounty raised from $1M to $10M
ibs_note: A single admin key had full control of the contracts holding user funds. A stolen key used directly (S1) leaves only on-chain controls: deny-by-default with timelocks on admin functions (C2), withdrawal budgets (C3) and a pausing watcher (C4). If an insider did it, S3 applies.
disputed: Access path: insider (CEO, to CoinDesk) vs external attacker (Bit Jungle). Date given as Oct 29 (Halborn) and Oct 30 (BXH, CoinDesk)

access: A stolen private key compromised two hot wallets (CEO Sheldon Xia); how it was obtained was not disclosed
detection: PeckShield reported it on Dec 4-5; BitMart paused withdrawals
response: Withdrawals paused; BitMart compensated affected users from its own funds
ibs_note: Hot-wallet key theft (S1), so the signer's checks are bypassed. Per-window budgets (C3) on the hot wallets and a watcher with freeze (C4) are the controls that limit it.
disputed: Loss: about $150M (BitMart) vs about $196M (PeckShield; CertiK about $195M)

access: The attacker exploited Vulcan Forged's servers, obtained its credentials for the wallet provider Venly, and used them to extract the private keys of 96 users' semi-custodial wallets (CEO Jamie Thomson). Venly said its own systems were not compromised
detection: Same day; Vulcan Forged announced it on Dec 12-13
response: Vulcan Forged promised to replace the stolen PYR from its treasury (about half reimbursed within days) and to move to non-custodial wallets
ibs_note: The keys were exported through the platform's credentials and then used directly (S1). Signer checks cannot act once keys leave the signer. Counterfactual: with non-exportable keys behind an IBS-checked signing API, the same stolen credentials could only request signatures, a signing-request attack that C1 and C3 address.
disputed: The DeFiLlama dataset classifies the victim as a DeFi protocol. The stolen keys belonged to users' wallets that the platform managed, so the catalog places it in U1

access: The Solana program's signature check used a deprecated instruction loader without an address check, so the attacker passed a forged verification and minted 120,000 wETH without guardian signatures
detection: Same day; exploited 18:24-18:28 UTC, patched 00:33 UTC Feb 3
response: Jump Crypto replenished 120,000 ETH; a $10M bounty was offered
ibs_note: Verification bug (S2); the guardians never signed. A per-window budget (C3) on the Ethereum-side unlock would still have capped the 93,750 ETH bridged back, whatever the cause.

victim: Ronin Network bridge (Sky Mavis / Axie Infinity)
access: Penetration of Sky Mavis IT infrastructure (social engineering reported); a stale Axie DAO allowlist arrangement let the attacker obtain the fifth validator signature via a gas-free RPC node
detection: Six days later (March 29), after a user could not withdraw 5,000 ETH; no monitoring had detected the drain
response: Bridge and Katana DEX halted; validator set enlarged; FBI attribution to Lazarus Group
ibs_note: Withdrawals were signed by compromised validator keys, so a signer-side check bound to source-chain deposit evidence (the bridge's equivalent of an intent, C1) is the relevant control, and the six-day detection gap is the clearest case for an independent reconciling watcher (C4). IBS does not prevent theft of the keys themselves.

access: Compromise of multisig signer keys, likely via social engineering of team members (Elliptic)
detection: Same day; Harmony announced the theft June 23-24
response: FBI attribution to Lazarus Group and APT38 (Jan 23, 2023); part of the funds frozen
ibs_note: Two stolen keys sufficed under a low multisig threshold. IBS cannot stop theft of signing keys; per-withdrawal intent binding to deposit evidence (C1, if enforced on-chain or by every signer), exposure budgets (C3) and a watcher (C4) limit and detect the drain.
disputed: Multisig threshold reported as 2-of-5 (Mudit Gupta via The Block) and 2-of-4 (PeckShield via The Record)

access: A routine upgrade initialized the trusted root to 0x00, so any unproven message counted as proven; once the first exploit appeared, many others copied its transaction
detection: Same day; Nomad identified the attack at about 17:32 ET
response: Forensics firms and law enforcement engaged; part of the funds returned later
ibs_note: Contract initialization bug (S2) exploited by many copycats; no signer was involved. A per-window outflow budget (C3) on the bridge would have bounded the free-for-all.

access: The admin address of Wintermute's DeFi vault was a vanity address generated with Profanity, whose 32-bit seed made the key recoverable by brute force (disclosed by 1inch on Sept 15). Wintermute had moved ETH out of the address but had not removed its admin rights
detection: Same day; the CEO announced the loss on Sept 20
response: Wintermute said it remained solvent; Amber Group reproduced the key recovery in 48 hours on a laptop
ibs_note: Weak key generation, which is outside IBS, gave the attacker a raw admin key, used directly on the vault (S1). On-chain withdrawal budgets (C3) and a watcher (C4) limit such a drain. Revoking the privileges of keys made by a generator known to be flawed is key hygiene, also outside IBS.
disputed: The DeFiLlama dataset classifies the incident as phishing; every source found attributes it to the Profanity key weakness

access: A forged IAVL range proof was accepted by the BSC Token Hub's proof verifier (CVE-2023-27575); the attacker first registered as a relayer and then withdrew 1,000,000 BNB twice
detection: Same day
response: Validators halted BNB Chain; about $100M-110M had moved off-chain before the halt; patched Oct 11
ibs_note: Proof-verification bug (S2). Containment came from halting the chain, a chain-level analogue of C4 that kept most of the minted BNB on BNB Chain; most bridges cannot do this. Loss is counted at the attacker's first address (S4).

chains: Not itemized in the sources used
access: SIM swap of an FTX employee's AT&T phone account, using a fake ID, which gave the co-conspirators the employee's authentication codes and access to company accounts (indictment, Jan 2024)
detection: Same day; the transfers happened Nov 11-12, hours after FTX filed for Chapter 11
response: Three people indicted (filed Jan 24, 2024)
ibs_note: The identity taken over was an employee's, not a user's, and how the transfers were then signed (internal tooling or exported keys) is not public. If they went through the exchange's own systems, intents authenticated independently of the employee's phone-based 2FA (C1) and per-window budgets (C3) would block or cap $400M in two days. If keys were exported, S1 applies.
attacker_model: A1-like if through internal tooling; A6 if keys (not public)
disputed: Victim identity. The indictment names "Victim Company-1"; Bloomberg (two people familiar with the case) and Elliptic identify it as FTX

access: Multichain's MPC node servers ran under the CEO's personal cloud account. The CEO was detained by Chinese police on May 21, 2023, with his computers, phones, hardware wallets and mnemonic phrases. The team says the July 7 transfers came from an IP address in Kunming
detection: Same day; PeckShield, SlowMist, Lookonchain and CertiK flagged the outflows
response: Multichain ceased operations on July 14. The CEO's sister, who had moved remaining funds to addresses she controlled on July 9, was also detained
ibs_note: One person held every MPC share, which defeats any signer-side control. Whether this was theft, insider action (S3) or a seizure is unresolved. On-chain budgets (C3) and a watcher (C4) are the only IBS controls that do not depend on the key holder.
attacker_model: none (insider or seizure, S3) or A6
disputed: Cause. Multichain's account implies access through the seized devices; Chainalysis describes a hack or a rug pull by insiders. Date: July 6 (Chainalysis) vs July 7 (Multichain, DeFiLlama)

access: The database of Mixin's cloud service provider was attacked, which gave the attacker access to the network's hot wallets (Mixin; Halborn). Details are not public
detection: Mixin announced it on Sept 25 and suspended deposits and withdrawals
response: Google and SlowMist engaged; Mixin offered the attacker a $20M bounty
ibs_note: Key material, or the ability to sign, was reachable from a cloud database; if raw keys were taken, S1 applies. The signing path is not public. Per-window budgets on the hot wallets (C3) and a watcher (C4) limit such a drain.
disputed: Amount: Mixin gives about $200M; PeckShield traced about $141M. The dataset classifies the victim as "Other"; Mixin held assets for users on its mainnet, so the catalog places it in U1

access: Hot-wallet private keys most likely leaked; Lazarus Group suspected (Halborn; X-explore). The attack transactions used the legacy transaction type, unlike Poloniex's normal EIP-1559 withdrawals (X-explore)
detection: Same day; PeckShield and Cyvers flagged it; Poloniex disabled its wallet about half an hour after the drain began
response: Wallet disabled; owner pledged full reimbursement; a white-hat bounty was offered
ibs_note: The transaction-type mismatch indicates the keys were used outside Poloniex's own signer (S1). A watcher checking outflows against the intent ledger (C4) would flag such transactions at once, and an on-chain budget (C3) bounds what leaves in the half hour before response.
disputed: Loss: about $114M (early estimate) to $126M

access: The private key of the contract deployer address was compromised (PeckShield; Elliptic: likely). The attacker added a new minter and minted PLA twice
detection: Same day (PeckShield, Feb 9)
response: PlayDapp offered a $1M bounty on Feb 10. The attacker minted again on Feb 12 (1.59B PLA). The contract was paused on Feb 13, and the token migrated
ibs_note: A stolen deployer key used directly (S1). The decisive gap was the three days between detection and pause, during which the second and larger mint happened. A watcher that freezes on an unexpected minter-role grant (C4), timelocked role changes (C2) and a mint budget (C3) would have stopped at least the second mint.
disputed: Loss measure. $290M is the market value of 1.79B newly minted PLA at pre-hack prices, against a prior supply of 577M; the attacker could sell only a fraction (ImmuneBytes: about $32M)

access: Social engineering of an employee at Ginco (DMM's wallet-software provider) via a fake LinkedIn recruiter and a malicious "pre-employment test" script (March 2024); stolen session cookies used to impersonate the employee (mid-May)
detection: Unauthorized outflow detected by DMM Bitcoin on May 31, 2024
response: FBI/DC3/Japan NPA attribution (TraderTraitor) on Dec 23-24, 2024; DMM Bitcoin agreed to transfer accounts and assets to SBI VC Trade (Dec 2, 2024)
ibs_note: Law enforcement states the attackers manipulated a legitimate transaction request from a DMM employee, which is the signing-request manipulation class IBS targets; binding the signature to an independently issued intent (C1) and a per-transaction exposure limit (C3) apply directly.
disputed: Loss given as $305M or $308M depending on valuation time

access: Disputed: WazirX attributes it to a discrepancy in the custody provider Liminal's interface; Liminal attributes it to three compromised WazirX devices
detection: Same day; WazirX halted withdrawals
response: Withdrawals halted; police report, FIU and CERT-In notified; WazirX ended its relationship with Liminal (Aug 14)
ibs_note: Signers approved a transaction whose displayed details differed from its contents (both parties agree on the mismatch, not on its origin). An independent intent check on the actual payload and default denial of contract upgrades would apply in either version.
disputed: Root cause (Liminal UI vs WazirX devices) is disputed between the two firms; the Grant Thornton review commissioned by Liminal found no compromise of Liminal's web application

access: Malware delivered via Telegram (impersonated former contractor, Sep 11) compromised at least three developers' devices
detection: Security monitoring alerts fired (ownership transfer, contract upgrade) during the attack
response: Lending markets paused; Mandiant engaged; signer set reduced to 7 with a 4-of-7 threshold
ibs_note: Hardware wallets blind-signed payloads replaced by malware while the interface showed legitimate data; ownership transfer of the lending pool provider is exactly the operation a deny-by-default policy (C2) would refuse without a dedicated, independently issued intent; alerts existed, so autonomous containment (C4) is the comparison point.
disputed: Loss reported as about $50M (post-mortem) to $53M (including approvals drained)

access: Supply chain: a Safe{Wallet} developer workstation was compromised (Feb 4, via a malicious Docker project per Safe); attacker used its AWS access to inject JavaScript into the Safe{Wallet} front end served from S3
detection: Bybit detected unauthorized activity during the routine cold-to-hot transfer, same day
response: FBI attribution (TraderTraitor/Lazarus) on Feb 26; malicious JavaScript removed by the attacker minutes after the theft
ibs_note: Signers approved what the tampered interface showed. IBS would require the signed payload to match an independently issued intent (the planned transfer to Bybit's hot wallet) and deny the delegatecall/implementation change by default; this holds only if the IBS check runs outside the compromised interface and signer workstations.
disputed: Loss figures range $1.4B-$1.5B by source and valuation time

access: Unauthorized access to a privileged management address (key compromise likely; how it was obtained is not public)
detection: Same day; Cyvers flagged the transactions; UPCX suspended deposits and withdrawals
response: Operations suspended; stolen tokens initially remained at the recipient address
ibs_note: A stolen admin key upgraded the ProxyAdmin and called withdrawByAdmin on three management accounts. IBS cannot stop a stolen key used directly on-chain; on-chain policy (timelocked upgrades, C2), withdrawal limits (C3) and upgrade monitoring with automatic pause (C4) limit it.
attacker_model: none (direct key use; on-chain policy not yet modelled)

access: Compromise of the project multisig (private key leak reported); attacker executed delegateCall, removed the admin role and added itself as owner
detection: Same day; Cyvers and on-chain observers flagged it
response: Exchanges froze much of the stolen assets; token migration to a new fixed-supply contract
ibs_note: Multisig control was seized and used to drain stablecoins and mint tokens. Default denial of delegateCall/owner changes (C2) and outflow limits with automatic containment (C3, C4) apply; how signing authority was obtained is not public, so C1's relevance is unknown.
disputed: Loss $11.3M (Cyvers) vs more than $30M (Hacken) vs about $41M including minted-token sales (Rekt)

access: Months-long social engineering of contributors, including in-person contact at crypto conferences (Drift); attackers prepared durable-nonce transactions from March 23
detection: Same day; the drain completed within about 12-20 minutes of the admin takeover
response: Deposits and withdrawals suspended; Drift attributes the attack (medium-high confidence) to UNC4736 (AppleJeus/Citrine Sleet); Elliptic and TRM report DPRK indicators
ibs_note: Security Council members signed admin-transfer transactions weeks earlier believing them harmless; Solana durable nonces kept those signatures valid indefinitely. Intent binding with an expiry and a declared purpose (C1), default denial of admin transfer and withdrawal-limit removal (C2), and exposure limits (C3) apply; IBS would have to run at each council signer, outside the attacker-influenced workflow.
disputed: Loss $280M (Drift) to $285-286M (PeckShield, Elliptic); dataset lists $295M. Dataset technique "Proxy Upgrade Hijack" understates the signing-path cause

chains: Ethereum (rsETH OFT adapter); stranded rsETH on about 20 chains
access: A LayerZero Labs developer was socially engineered through a malicious GitHub repository (Mar 6). Harvested session keys gave the attacker LayerZero's cloud and RPC environment. Two internal op-geth RPC nodes were poisoned in memory, and external RPC providers were hit by DoS so the DVN relied on the poisoned nodes (LayerZero report)
detection: Kelp paused its contracts 46 minutes after the exploit at 17:35 UTC (CoinDesk)
response: Two follow-up attempts to unlock another 40,000 rsETH reverted. Arbitrum's Security Council froze 30,766 ETH (about $71M). Kelp later refilled 117,132 rsETH from Aave and Kelp recovery funds
ibs_note: No key was stolen. The DVN signed a fabricated source-chain event with its legitimate keys after its RPC read path was poisoned, and the application's 1-of-1 DVN setting left no second verifier. This is IBS's target class, with one finding: the forged input was the evidence the signer treats as authorization, so C1 holds only if the intent authority reads the source chain through a path the attacker cannot control. A per-window budget (C3) would have capped an unlock of 18% of supply, and the 46-minute pause (C4) blocked the follow-up attempts.
disputed: Who chose the 1-of-1 setting. LayerZero says Kelp changed a 2-of-2 configuration to 1-of-1; Kelp says 1-of-1 was LayerZero's shipped default

access: A bug in how Elements cached range-proof validation let the attacker create about 3,998.5 unbacked L-BTC, which were redeemed for real BTC through a peg-out that looked legitimate and was signed by the federation's 11-of-15 multisig. No peg-out key was compromised (SideSwap; Liquid)
detection: Same day; Liquid halted new transactions on Sept 6
response: Patch deployed by 01:09 UTC Sept 7. Self-described white hats returned about 3,400 BTC (about $262M-270M) and kept about 598.5 BTC (about $47M). Block production resumed on Sept 10 with Elements v23.3.4
ibs_note: A validation bug in node software (S2); the federation's signers signed a peg-out that the buggy rules accepted. Not a signer compromise, but notable: one peg-out took about 95% of reserves. A per-window exposure budget enforced by the signers (C3) would have capped it, whatever the cause.

chains: Ethereum, BNB Chain, Avalanche, Tron, Zcash and others
access: Breach of a critical backend system within the exchange's wallet infrastructure (CEO statement)
detection: Bitget's security systems detected unauthorized transfers at 18:31 UTC, Sept 24, 2026
response: Withdrawals suspended and resumed in phases from Sept 28; loss covered by the User Protection Fund (over $464M); CEO attributes the attack to North Korea based on on-chain analysis and IP patterns
ibs_note: Per the CEO, attackers spoofed transaction data and triggered Bitget's own authorization and signing process, which is the signing-request manipulation class IBS targets; intent binding (C1) and exposure budgets on hot/warm tiers (C3) apply directly. Root-cause report details beyond the CEO statement not yet reviewed.
disputed: Loss revised from $351.6M to $387.5M after tracing Zcash and Tron assets; attribution is the company's, not law enforcement's

chains: Ethereum and about nine other chains (10 total), including XRP, Arbitrum
access: Attacker reached a service container in Binance's withdrawal/signing infrastructure (reported); attacker infrastructure funded via Tornado Cash on Oct 28
detection: Same evening; hot wallet emptied 20:20-20:24 UTC; deposits and withdrawals paused
response: Stablecoin issuers froze funds (Tether about 971M USDT, Circle about 823M USDC); Arbitrum Security Council moved about $30M; Binance reports about $3B frozen and states it found no evidence of private key leak and will cover losses
ibs_note: The reference incident for this research: the exchange's own signer signed EIP-7702 delegations and withdrawals requested by compromised orchestration. Reproduced in the testbed (A1); IBS configurations R2-R4 contained it in simulation and on Besu (see testbed/results).
disputed: Total loss estimates $6.3B (Binance) and $6.36B (TRM Labs, via Wikipedia); attribution to TraderTraitor reported but not confirmed by law enforcement as of 2026-10-31
